inline_comments.comment: Both `watchFile(generation, 'head', gitDir, ...)` (line 132) and `watchFile(generation, 'packedRefs', gitDir, ...)` (this line) register independent `FSWatcher` instances on the exact same `gitDir` path. The Node.js `fs.watch` API delivers each OS directory-change event to every watcher registered on that path, so any change within `.git/` (e.g., when `.git/HEAD` changes on a branch switch, or when `.git/packed-refs` is updated) will fire both watcher callbacks. The result is two back-to-back `emitGitStateChange()` calls for a single logical git event. Debouncing in the consumer absorbs the duplicate, but the `head` watcher's `configureBranchWatcher()` is also called on packed-refs changes where it is unneeded. This production behaviour is not reflected in the tests, which simulate individual watcher fires in isolation. Consider consolidating these into a single directory watcher that dispatches based on the changed filename passed to the `fs.watch` listener, or watch the specific files (e.g. `join(gitDir, 'HEAD')` and `join(gitDir, 'packed-refs')`) rather than the parent directory.

`void this.configureBranchWatcher(gitDir, generation)` is a fire-and-forget async call inside a synchronous watcher callback. If `configureBranchWatcher` rejects — for example, because `readHeadRef` encounters a non-ENOENT file-read error on a corrupted repo — the rejection is silently dropped and may emit an `unhandledRejection` event in Node.js. The same pattern repeats in the branch watcher's `onChange` closure inside `configureBranchWatcher` itself (~line 215). Consider adding `.catch((err) => { ... })` with at minimum a `logger.debug` or `logger.warn` call so failures surface instead of disappearing silently.

The `catch {}` block in `setupWatchers` swallows every error without any logging. The intent ('opportunistic watching') is explained in the comment, but unexpected errors — permissions failures, programming mistakes — are completely invisible. Because the `finally` block already guards `watcherSetupInFlight`, adding a `logger.debug('Change detection git watcher setup failed', error)` inside the catch has no behavioural cost and would significantly aid future debugging.

`match[1]` from the gitdir-pointer regex is passed directly to `resolvePath` without trimming. The `.trim()` call on `gitPointer` normalises the outer string but does not strip whitespace that may appear at the end of the matched line itself (e.g. `gitdir: ../worktrees/foo  ` with trailing spaces). If such a path is resolved and then used for `stat` or `watch` calls, the filesystem operations will fail with ENOENT. Using `match[1].trim()` is a cheap, defensive fix. The same consideration applies to `match?.[1]` in `readHeadRef` (~line 304), where a trailing-space branch name would produce a malformed path in `join(gitDir, branchRef)`.

`void callback` is an unusual idiom for suppressing an unused-parameter lint warning. The standard TypeScript convention is to prefix the parameter name with an underscore — `_callback` — which is recognised by TypeScript's compiler (`noUnusedParameters`) and by common linters without requiring a runtime expression. This also makes the intent immediately clear to future readers.

The test "watches git and branch directories for git state changes" fires `watchRecords[0]` (the `head` watcher) and `watchRecords[1]` (the `packedRefs` watcher) independently and expects one `onGitStateChange` call per emission. In production, because both watchers are registered on the same `gitDir` path, a single OS change event for `.git/HEAD` would trigger both watcher callbacks in the same turn, producing two `onGitStateChange` calls. The test's mock setup fires each `FSWatcher` in isolation, so this double-notification behaviour is never validated against or caught. A test that calls `watchRecords[0].emitChange()` and asserts the callback count afterwards would accurately reflect the real behaviour.

general_comments.comment: The `gitDiffProvider` option type in `ChangeDetectionService` was widened from `Pick<GitDiffProvider, 'getChangedFiles' | 'getRepoRoot'>` to the concrete `GitDiffProvider` class. The `Pick` was a lightweight structural contract: any object with those two methods qualified. The change implicitly adds `onGitStateChange` to the required surface, which is correct, but the concrete-class type forces callers supplying a custom provider to either subclass `GitDiffProvider` or match its full implementation (as `MockGitDiffProvider` does). Extracting a `GitDiffProvider` interface — or at minimum a `Pick<GitDiffProvider, 'getChangedFiles' | 'getRepoRoot' | 'onGitStateChange'>` — would make the required contract explicit and allow lightweight alternative implementations (e.g. a polling-based or no-op provider) without inheriting the class's internal watcher machinery.
